content: You are reinventing the query model, specifically for TMs. Fwiw I already wrote a random sample oracle and a way to compose it with other oracles. A non deterministic oracle is the same. Instead of using a probability measure, you supply an existential proposition for a non deterministic computation, and extract the data with choice.
What is the underlying computation model you use (the "inner" machine)?
Specified by user. Are you asking about the random oracle model or the non deterministic oracle model?

Ok but that's still the bulk of the work, isn't it? And it has to "match" the resource model of Turing machines. I'm mainly interested in the sub-linear space model, but the model should not matter, I think.

I am not sure I fully understand what you mean, but in my model of Turing machines I discard explicit transition functions. Instead I describe the entire TM like an algorithm in lean code. At the nuts and bolts level of deterministic TMs, you can move tape heads, read or write to cells under the tape heads, and change states.

Fwiw you still need the underlying TM model because basic complexity theory is fairly finicky about details like encodings of input and padded inputs and such. In fact I had a chat on discord about this and the conclusion was that we should just define the three common variants of space complexity that I found. They are all used in different ways and are subtly different.
I know that's why I say that the resource consumption model should be equivalent (linear in space and polynomial in time) to that of Turing machines
I am challenging the premise that there even is a single well defined model
I think we are again moving away too much from the topic of this thread. My main point was that we can use e.g. the single-tape TM we already have to define logspace.
How does your model change single tape TMs to allow logspace?
It does not change them, it uses them: They are used as the inner machine model. But we can also use lambda calculus if we want.

That’s when you stop doing textbook complexity. That’s why my point is relevant. Concretely, logspace classes are defined in a very specific way with TMs to facilitate certain intuitions. If you use a slightly different version of the definitions, proofs of theorems like L \subseteq P break down.

Texbook complexity is super hand-wavy and makes a big step from actual Turing machines to describing logspace algorithms. I'm not saying we should not prove equivalence between a textbook multi-tape TM and the one proposed above, but my proposal is to use a model like the one above for the actual upper-bound proofs.

Then you have my query model. You give a time and space cost to these machines and use them in other TMs. If you really want to explicitly specify them, you can reduce your models to the Single/Multi tape TM models. But this is not strictly necessary.

I already have collaborators and students working on tm and circuit complexity upper bounds in this query model. I explicitly wrote my PRs and later started Algolean to address this exact issue in algorithms and complexity, that low level models are tedious to work with. The idea is, you take the annoying TM (or even RAM) operations whose complexity you know (and wish to fix), and encode them as queries with those complexities (such as your preferred loglogspace machine). Practically every model under the sun is a query model.

17 messages were moved here from #CSLib > Computation model for sub-linear space, nondeterminism, etc by Chris Henson.

@Chris Henson I find this exceptionally irritating that you moved a discussion that is pertinent to CSLib. They are conceptually reinventing what I have already designed and implemented and I am pointing it out*. In fact they’re solving the exact issue that I have already solved.

*this is not a bad thing, good ideas come up again and again, that’s a sign of robustness and a source of further insight.

As you have pointed out youself many times before, you are not the domain expert on this topic. As it happens, I am. I would be extremely grateful if I was not subject to such repeatedly uninformed decisions by you.

While there are connections between your query model and what I posted, the point was to illustrate that we can re-use the single tape Turing machine without modification to define logspace computations and how we do this. At the same time there can, but there does not have to be a big formalism involved. I do not claim authorship of any ideas (I find that concept bizarre to begin with) but I think “reinventing the same concept” and “solving the exact same issue” is kind of a stretch here.
You mentioned that complexity theorists don’t go into details to specify algorithms or TMs
That is the problem I am solving.

And you suggested options for randomised and non deterministic computations. Again I am solving them. I am not discussing any authorship issues here (although academia is literally built on that idea). It’s a good sign that the same idea shows up as a solution in different domains.

Anyway. My point is, I’d like to understand how your model differs from an oracle set up and how it solves the logspace issue. For example how would we define L and NL in single tape TMs using this model? How would reductions work? To me it sounds like this model makes an oracle call to another single tape tm which serves as a work tape. Another possibility is we can entirely replace this oracle with a lean function + associated costs. I think it will be easier to compare code once we both finalise our designs.

I think the oracle view is confusing here. In an oracle setting, the resource costs of the oracle are usually ignored, while in my proposal, both the space and the time consumption of both machines are counted. I would also not know which of the two machines would be the base machine and which would be the oracle. It's more like two machines interacting and passing messages. Also the behaviour of the outer machine is always fixed. It's more like putting an "engine" onto an existing machine.

With multi-tape Turing machines, you usually restrict the way certain tapes can be used: The input tape is read-only, but the head can move freely within the input. The output tape is write-only and the head has to move to the right after writing. A nondeterminism tape is read-only and the head can only move to the right etc.

My proposal replaces these tapes by a fixed mechanism that "drives" the inner machine.

The space used by such an "enhanced" machine (let's use that term for now) is the max space used by the inner machine across all iterations.

And I would define L relative to a machine model and it's definition of space: A language is in L if there is a machine that accepts the language and there are two natural numbers a and b such that for all n and all inputs of length n, the space usage on this input is at most a * (log n) + b.

Now if you just count the number of non-empty cells across the execution of a single-tape TM, you will always get at least a linear space usage. It might be possible to discount original input characters etc but it's no fun and nondeterminism is even harder. But if the single-tape Turing machine is enhanced in this way, it can capture L.

But we can use much more convenient computational models than the single-tape Turing machine, as long as they have a "compatible" resource measure (linear relation to a single-tape TM wrt space and polynomial relation wrt time).

So to summarize: We can "enhance" any computational model that just needs to be able to tell for an arbitrary lean function what its resource consumption is (relative to an encoding). The model does not need to be able to reach down to logspace. And from this enhancement we automatically get sub-linear space, nondeterminism, alteration, oracles etc. - without having to define how these things work inside the model.

But yes, maybe I can write some concrete code if I find the time.

I agree that concrete code will help. But fwiw one can count oracles costs in various ways. This trick has come up in other contexts in the PL and crypto literature. One can also model normal sequential algorithms by peeling off complex subalgorithms as oracles and giving them input-dependent costs.

As I understand it, Shreyas was (temporarily, I hope) banned for his comments here. An increasing number of users of this Zulip are becoming concerned about the rather heavy-handed approach of the CoC committee and there's been a good bit of discussion (elsewhere, obviously...).

This makes me uncomfortable.

Dear Alex, speaking as a member of the Code of Conduct.

We understand that this can feel uncomfortable, and I appreciate people raising concerns about how the CoC process is perceived. That said, we cannot discuss individual moderation cases publicly, including the case mentioned here. This is important both for the privacy of the people involved and for the integrity of the process. For the same reason, public speculation about particular cases is not something we can really answer in detail. What I can say is that decisions of this kind are not taken lightly, and they are not made unilaterally. The CoC committee discusses them carefully, and serious moderation decisions are made in agreement with the maintainers. More generally, if people have concerns about the way the CoC is being applied, we do want to hear them. The best way to do that is to contact the CoC committee or the maintainers privately, so that concerns can be discussed responsibly without turning any individual case into a public debate. Of course, even in private we will not discuss the details of a specific case with people who are not directly involved, but we can listen to broader concerns about the process and take them seriously.
if the moderation reasoning and decisions will not be made public, how can the moderation ever be perceived as fair?

I understand the concern, but I am not sure there is a way to make individual moderation decisions fully public that would actually be fair. For example, we cannot publicly say “person X was banned for reason Y” and then explain the reports, context, private discussions, or previous interactions that led to the decision. Doing so would effectively create a public trial every time a CoC issue is reported. That would be bad for the person who reported the issue, bad for the person being reported, and bad for the community as a whole. This means that individual cases cannot be completely transparent. The alternative is procedural trust: serious decisions are discussed carefully, are not made unilaterally, and are taken in agreement with the maintainers/moderators. That is the mechanism meant to prevent arbitrary or unfair decisions. We are very open to hearing general concerns about the CoC process, including concerns that it is being applied too heavily. But we cannot make the details of particular cases public, and we cannot have a public debate every time a possible violation is reported. Of course, the community guidelines themselves are public and can be found here.
